1:
After Zophar has emptied his quiver, Job takes up the reply that will run through this chapter and the two that follow, and the witnesses first mark the change in his temper. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sets the scene: each of the three friends has now supplied his quota, and Job proceeds to answer the third, showing himself far more conversant with the wisdom and majesty of God than they are, though in their own esteem they alone are wise. The reformed John Gill reads the opening formula more soberly still, as simply a reply to Zophar and a defence of himself, the substance of which fills this and the next two chapters.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears in the whole answer a rebuke to the proud and scornful. Job's friends had carried themselves as men who held the monopoly of wisdom, and nothing, Henry says, is more weak and unbecoming, nor better deserves to be ridiculed, than to think oneself wiser than all mankind besides. Yet Henry weighs honestly whether the reproof was just: he will not think the friends designed Job any abuse, for they aimed to convince him and so, in the right method, to comfort him; and he grants that we are apt to call reproofs reproaches, and to think ourselves mocked when we are only advised and admonished. Still there was colour for the charge, and Henry lets Job feel the peculiar bitterness of being trodden on when he is down, and suspected of it too readily by a heart already sore.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke lays out the architecture of the reply as an argument and not a mere outburst. Job reproves the boasting of his friends and shows their uncharitableness toward himself in the opening verses; he then asserts that even the tabernacles of robbers prosper, and yet that God remains the Governor of the world — a truth proclaimed, Clarke says, by all parts of the creation, whether animate or inanimate, and by the revolutions that overtake states and kingdoms. So the witnesses read the chapter's first word as the hinge on which the book turns from the friends' confident theology to Job's harder and deeper vision: that the ways of God are wider and darker than any of Zophar's neat accountings, and that the man on the ash-heap has looked further into them than the three who came to teach him.
2:
"No doubt but ye are the people, and wisdom shall die with you" — and the witnesses are unanimous that the words drip with irony. The reformed John Gill will not let the sentence be taken seriously: Job does not mean that his friends are merely of the common sort, but ridicules their vast self-conceit, as if they were "the people," the only men of consequence in the world for sense and wisdom, the sole men of reason and understanding, all others being but fools and asses — a stroke Gill hears aimed back at Zophar's gibe about the wild ass's colt. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke puts it plainly: "Doubtless ye are the wisest men in the world; all wisdom is concentrated in you; and when ye die, there will no more be found on the face of the earth. This is a strong irony."

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch weigh the grammar of the taunt. The admission is strengthened by a particle meaning "truly then," and is meant ironically: ye are not merely a few individuals but "the people," the whole race of men, as the word is used in Isaiah 40:7, so that all human understanding is shut up in you, and when once you die it will seem to have died out with you. They note that the Septuagint caught the sense — "are ye alone men?" — and, coming to the next line, they reject Ewald's rendering "I also have a head even as you" as a western, modern, and unbiblical turn; the Hebrew says heart, the seat of understanding, not head.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the irony to the same effect — you have engrossed all the reason of mankind, and each of you carries as much wisdom as a whole people put together, so that all the world's wisdom lives in you and will be utterly lost when you die. But Wesley lifts a sober truth out of the sarcasm: when wise and good men do die, it is a comfort to think that wisdom and goodness do not die with them, and it is folly to imagine any great, irreparable loss of us when we are gone, since God keeps the fulness of the Spirit still in his own hand and can raise up others more fit to do his work. So the witnesses hold the verse together as pure irony with a grave lesson folded inside it: the conceit that wisdom is one's private freehold is exposed by the very God who keeps its whole store in his own hand.
3:
Job answers the imagined monopoly by staking his own claim — "I have understanding as well as you; I am not inferior to you" — and the witnesses read the retort as vindication rather than boast. The reformed John Gill takes the "understanding" in two ranges: a natural understanding of natural things, which parts a man from a brute, and a spiritual understanding, enlightened by the Spirit of God, by which Job knew himself and his state by nature, and knew God, and knew his living Redeemer who should stand upon the earth in the latter day both to redeem him and to judge him, and knew his own interest in him and in the blessings of grace and glory. The alternative rendering "I have a heart as well as you" Gill fills out to the same purpose — a wise and upright heart, sincere and devoid of hypocrisy, as good as any of theirs.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke presses the second clause and the sting in its tail: "I do not fall short of any of you in understanding, wisdom, learning, and experience." As for the things they have so gravely delivered, "who knoweth not such things as these?" — all their boasted wisdom, Clarke says, consists only in strings of proverbs that are in every person's mouth, and are no proof of wisdom or experience in those who use them. John Wesley guards Job from the charge of vanity: he says this not in a way of boasting but for the just vindication both of himself and of that cause of God which, for the substance of it, he maintained rightly, as God himself attests in Job 42:7.

Wesley then turns the common ground into a rebuke of the whole dispute. The truth is, he has Job say, neither you nor I have any reason to be puffed up with our knowledge of these things, for the most barbarous nations know that God is infinite in wisdom, and power, and justice — "but this is not the question between you and me." There the witnesses converge. Job is not disputing the greatness of God, which the friends parade as though it were their discovery; he grants it more fully than they, and complains only that they mistake commonplaces for arguments and press truisms as if they settled his case. The wisdom the friends monopolize is the wisdom everyone has; the real question — why the upright man is broken while robbers thrive — they have not so much as touched.
4:
"I am as one mocked of his neighbour" — and the witnesses feel the double edge of the complaint, that the scorn comes from friends and falls on a praying man. The reformed John Gill reports Sephorno's turn, that were Job to deny the truths of God's greatness he would be derided by all; but he prefers the plainer reading, that Job instances himself as living proof that good men are afflicted in this life. Once caressed in his prosperity, he is now the scorn and contempt of his neighbours, and even his mocking is no small part of his suffering — to endure cruel mockings has ever been the lot of the godly, and to be mocked by a friend aggravates the wound.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the middle clause as the sharpest thorn: "Though I am invoking God for help and salvation, yet my friends mock me in this most solemn and sacred work. But God answereth me." He owns the verse very difficult, on which no two critics agree, and lays out the wrestlings of Good, Coverdale, and Parkhurst before concluding, with a shrug, that "to emendations and conjectures there is no end." The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott frames the whole as a live question: "the laughing-stock of his companion — he who called on God, and He answered him." This is either the character Job claims for himself, or the supposed taunt of his friends; and Ellicott draws the maxim that closes the matter — "ridicule is no test of truth or of merit."

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley sharpens who the mockers are: not the profane, but Job's religious neighbours, "those who call upon God, and not in vain, whose prayers I covet, not their reproaches." And he lets Job own his standing under the scorn — "the just: I, who, notwithstanding all their hard censures, dare still own it, that through God's grace I am an upright man." So the witnesses gather two griefs into one line. It is bitter that the men who deride Job are themselves men of prayer, whose good opinion he would gladly have; and it is bitter that the very uprightness for which God will vindicate him is the thing they laugh to scorn. That a just man who cries to God and is heard should be a byword to his own companions is, for these witnesses, the ancient and standing lot of the righteous, and no proof at all against them.
5:
The picture of the fallen man despised by the comfortable — "as a lamp despised in the thought of him that is at ease" — is a knot the witnesses openly labour at. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confesses the received words "convey no sense," and offers two ways through. Either the lamp or torch made ready for feet that totter uncertain in the darkness is disregarded and rejected by those who are at ease and need no such aid — though then it is not clear why Job should liken himself to it; or, more probably, there is a settled contempt for calamity in the thoughts of the man at ease, a scorn kept ready at hand for those who are tottering with their feet. The reformed John Gill takes the slipping not as a fall into sin but into calamity, and reads Job as the very man "ready to slip," appointed to be the laughing-stock of the unstable and the secure.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley draws out the image with feeling: the man who slips with his feet and falls into trouble, "though he had formerly shone as a lamp, is then looked upon as a lamp going out, as the snuff of a candle, which we throw to the ground and tread upon," and so is despised in the thought of him that is at ease. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, folding this verse into Job's complaint of contempt, names the fault on the other side. It is the common sin of those who live in prosperity: being full, and easy, and merry themselves, they look scornfully upon the afflicted, overlook them, and study to forget them; wealth without grace makes men thus careless of their poor neighbours.

Henry turns it into a mirror. Even the just, upright man — a burning and shining light in his generation — if he enter into temptation or come under a cloud is looked upon with contempt, for poverty eclipses all a man's lustre, and lamps taken out of golden candlesticks and put, like Gideon's, into earthen pitchers are valued by nobody as before. So the witnesses converge on the cruelty the verse exposes even as they divide over its exact rendering. Whether the despised lamp is the neglected torch of the tottering or the contempt itself lying ready in the easy man's heart, all of them hear Job describing the world's settled way with the fallen: to those who stand secure, a good man's misfortune is not a summons to pity but an occasion for scorn.
6:
"The tabernacles of robbers prosper, and they that provoke God are secure" — and here Job lays down the fact that shatters his friends' whole theology. The reformed John Gill points the robbers at the Chaldeans and Sabeans who had plundered Job himself and lived on in fatness on the spoils of others; a hard fact, he grants, that has been a trial and temptation to good men in every age who struggle to reconcile it with the justice and wisdom of God. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke states the principle drawn from it: those who live by plunder are often found in great secular prosperity, and the impious live secure and affluent, so that "prosperity and adversity are no evidences of a man's spiritual state, nor of the place he holds in the approbation or disapprobation of God."

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets the verse squarely against Zophar, who had concluded that the eyes of the wicked shall fail in Job 11:20. Job opposes it flatly: God, in disposing men's outward affairs, acts as a sovereign, reserving the exact distribution of rewards and punishments for the future state. The sinners here are of the worst kind — robbers, and such as provoke God, blasphemers and persecutors — yet their very tabernacles prosper, a blessing seeming to run on into their families; they are secure, feeling no danger from providence or conscience; and into their hand God brings abundantly, more than heart could wish, as the psalmist owns in Psalm 73:7. "We cannot therefore judge of men's piety by their plenty," Henry concludes, "nor of what they have in their heart by what they have in their hand."

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott adds a note on the last clause, "into whose hand God bringeth abundantly." Some, he says, would render it "to him that bringeth his god in his hand," comparing the man of Habakkuk 1:11 whose might is his god; but Ellicott judges the common construction more in accordance with usage. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley states the thesis the verse serves: Job's friends had all supposed that wicked men cannot prosper long in the world, and this Job denies, maintaining that God herein acts as sovereign and reserves that exact reckoning for the other world. The witnesses do not divide over the fact, only feel its weight differently: the prosperity of robbers is not a flaw in providence to be explained away, but a standing proof that God's justice keeps a longer calendar than the friends will allow.
7:
Having stated the offensive fact, Job sends his teachers back to school under the dumb creatures — "ask now the beasts, and they shall teach thee; and the fowls of the air, and they shall tell thee." The reformed John Gill draws from the creatures the very lesson the friends deny: even among the beasts the harmless and useful fall a prey to the strong, sheep and lambs to lions and wolves, doves to the hawk, the lesser fish to the greater, so that the good are devoured while the ravenous thrive; and the flocks and herds serve wicked men more often than good, feeding the luxury of the oppressor. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the summons more simply as a rebuke to Zophar's pomp: what Zophar had uttered so gravely about God's infinite wisdom in Job 11:7, Job says, needs no journey into heaven or hell to learn — "thou mayst learn it even from the beasts."

The other wesleyan-arminian witness, Adam Clarke, gives the whole appeal its argumentative point through Good's fine paraphrase: "Why tell ye me that the Almighty hath brought this calamity upon me? Every thing in nature — the beasts of the field, the fowls of the heaven, every inhabitant of earth and sea — is the work of his hands, and feels and acknowledges him the universal Creator and Controller. It is the common doctrine of all nature; but to apply it as ye would apply it to me, and to assert that I am suffering from being guilty of hypocrisy, is equally impertinent." He ordains everything in wisdom as well as in power; but why good and evil are promiscuously scattered through nature and human life, Clarke has Job say, "ye are as ignorant of as myself."

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears the creatures teaching both truths at once — that the tabernacles of robbers prosper, since even in the brute world the greater devour the less and men are as the fishes of the sea in Habakkuk 1:14; and that the wisdom, power, and goodness of God, which Zophar had made so vast a mystery, lie open for any to read in the book of the creatures. From God's sovereign dominion over the inferior creatures, Henry says, we should learn to acquiesce in all his disposals of the affairs of the children of men, though they run contrary to our measures. So the witnesses agree that Job's appeal is no digression: he turns his learned friends into pupils of the ox and the sparrow, that the plainest creatures might teach what the wise men had failed to see — that the world's order is God's, and its riddles are his too.
8:
The roll of teachers widens to the ground and the sea — "speak to the earth, and it shall teach thee; and the fishes of the sea shall declare unto thee." The reformed John Gill bids the reader ask even "a sprig of the earth," any shrub or tree that grows out of it, and all will unite in one doctrine: that they are raised and preserved by the power of God, so many standing instances of his wisdom, power, and goodness. The lowest and most silent things in the world become, on Job's summons, witnesses more eloquent than the three friends who came with speeches.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch, gathering this verse into the strophe that runs down to the ear that tries words, fix the drift of the whole appeal against a mistaken reading. It is wrong, they argue, to make Job point the creatures at his own hard destiny, as if the beasts and the earth taught the lesson of his undeserved suffering; the movement of the passage runs the other way. What all these creatures teach and declare is the thing named in the lines that follow — that the hand of the LORD has wrought all this, and that in his hand is the soul of every living thing. The earth and the fish are called not to certify Job's misery but to certify the universal dominion of God, in whose grasp the whole living world is held.

So the witnesses read the verse as the turning of Job's argument from the disorder he has just pressed to the sovereignty that overrules it. He has said the plainest fact of the world is that robbers prosper; now he says the plainest fact of the world is also that God's hand has made and holds it all. Both truths are written on the same open page of creation, and neither cancels the other: the God who governs the ox and the fish and the growing shrub is the very God who lets the Sabean thrive and the upright fall, and the mystery Zophar thought so deep is one the dumb earth can teach. Gill lets the shrub and Keil and Delitzsch let the strophe carry the single point — that nothing in the whole creation lies outside the working of the hand about to be named, and that the friends' neat doctrine of desert is far too small to cover a world so wholly God's.
9:
The question that gathers up the whole appeal to the creatures — "who knoweth not in all these that the hand of the LORD hath wrought this?" — draws the witnesses less to its sense than to a single word in it, the covenant name of God. The reformed John Gill takes the opening as "who knoweth not by all these creatures": what man is so stupid and senseless that he cannot learn, even from irrational creatures, the very things Zophar discoursed of — God's power and wisdom and providence — since by the things that are made the invisible things of God are clearly seen and understood, his eternal power and Godhead, as Romans 1:20 declares.

But the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott seizes on what most readers pass by. This, he observes, "is the only place in the dialogue parts of Job in which the sacred name of Jehovah is found, and Job's very use of the word in such a context is the clearest evidence of the superior knowledge that he claims." None of his friends ever employs the covenant name; Job uses it here, and by it betrays a knowledge of God deeper than theirs — the God of the creatures is also the God of the covenant. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley confirms the point exactly: "this is the only time that we meet with the name Jehovah in all the discourses between Job and his friends, for God in that age was more known by the name Shaddai, the Almighty."

The witnesses do not divide; together they make the verse turn on a quiet marvel. In the midst of a chapter that presses the disorder of the world and the darkness of providence, Job lets slip the one name that binds the Maker of the beasts to the Keeper of promises — and lets it slip precisely where he is confessing that the hand behind all these things is the LORD's. That the sufferer who complains most bitterly of God's dealings should also be the one man in the debate who names him by his covenant name is, for these witnesses, no small thing: it shows that Job's quarrel is a believer's quarrel, and that beneath the hard question of the chapter lies a knowledge of God the three comforters, for all their orthodoxy, never reach. The hand that has wrought all this is not a blind fate but the LORD, and Job, even in his darkness, knows it.
10:
The ground of the whole appeal is laid bare — "in whose hand is the soul of every living thing, and the breath of all mankind" — and the witnesses read it as Job's resolving of all providence into God's absolute propriety in his creatures. The reformed John Gill takes the first clause of every animal, as distinct from man in the second: the life of each is from God, continued as long as he pleases, and not to be taken away without his leave, so that not one of two sparrows, worth but a farthing, falls to the ground without the knowledge and will of God, as the Saviour teaches in Matthew 10:29. Every breathing thing holds its life as a tenant at the will of its Maker.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke presses the two Hebrew phrases and hears in them a distinction. "The soul of every living thing" he renders literally the soul of all life, and "the breath of all mankind" the spirit or breath of all flesh; and he asks whether the first does not point to the immortal soul, the principle of all intellectual life, and the second to the breath, the respiration by which animal existence is continued, referring the reader back to the language of Job 10:1. Whether or not the distinction be pressed so far, the two clauses together sweep the whole scale of creaturely life, from the beast that perishes to the man made in God's image, into the one hand that holds them all.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the verse into its plainest force: all the creatures, and mankind particularly, derive their being from God, owe it to him, depend upon him for its support, lie at his mercy, are under his direction and dominion and entirely at his disposal, and at his summons must resign their lives. "All souls are his," Henry says; "and may he not do what he will with his own?" There the witnesses land as one. If the breath of every living thing is held in God's hand, then the disorder Job has pressed — robbers thriving, the upright broken — is no escape from God's government but a mystery within it; the God who could recall any life at a word is plainly free to order all lives as he will. Job does not soften the hard fact of the chapter; he roots it deeper, in a sovereignty so total that the very life by which men prosper or suffer is, moment by moment, a loan from the hand that made them.
11:
Job pauses to claim the right of judgment — "doth not the ear try words? and the mouth taste his meat?" — and the witnesses take the proverb as his demand to weigh what has been said rather than swallow it whole. The reformed John Gill reads the ear as trying articulate sounds, the mind judging by them whether a thing be right or wrong, true or false, to be received or rejected; so those who have spiritual ears try the words of God and of men, discern the wholesome words of Christ from the doctrines of false teachers, and bring all to the standard of the sanctuary. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke turns the same edge back on the friends: "all these are common-place sayings; ye have advanced nothing new; ye have cast no light upon the dispensations of Providence."

The grammatical-historical voices sharpen both the point and the grammar. Charles Ellicott hears Job answering the appeal to authority and tradition: it is given to the wise man not to accept everything he has received but to discriminate; and though wisdom be granted the prerogative of age, the true Ancient of Days must needs be wise indeed. Keil and Delitzsch fix the comparison in the words: the sayings of the ancients are not to be received without being proved, the connecting particle being one of likeness, so that the ear, used here as the organ of testing much as in Hebrews 5:14, has the task of searching out and trying weighty sayings, as the palate by tasting finds out what food is wholesome and fit.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gives the maxim its balance, taking it either as the close of the foregoing or the preface to what follows. The mind of man, he says, has as good a faculty of discerning between truth and error, when duly stated, as the palate has of discerning between sweet and bitter; and so Job demands the liberty to judge for himself of what the friends had said, and grants them the same liberty in judging of him, appealing to any impartial judgment to try the words on both sides. The witnesses do not divide, only vary the emphasis — Gill and Keil and Delitzsch on the testing of doctrine by a discerning ear, Clarke and Ellicott on the staleness of the friends' proverbs and the duty to sift tradition rather than bow to it. Together they make the verse Job's claim to a hearing: that truth is not settled by the weight of names or years, but must be tasted and tried, and that his case has not yet been so much as fairly weighed.
12:
The proverb of the aged — "with the ancient is wisdom, and in length of days understanding" — the witnesses read chiefly as a foil, a human wisdom set up only to be dwarfed by the divine wisdom of the verse that follows. The reformed John Gill turns over its bearing: Job does not mean himself, who was not very ancient, though Eliphaz seems so to have taken him; rather he may be wishing that some aged man would arbitrate the quarrel, or answering Bildad's counsel to search the fathers, allowing that wisdom is with them for the most part, yet only so far as their judgment agrees with the wisdom of God. Best of all, Gill thinks, it is a proverb generally granted — that men well advanced in years, having lived long and learned much by observation and experience, have commonly gathered a good share of wisdom.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch, opening the strophe on God's almighty power, let the concession stand only to be surpassed: it is allowed that with grey heads there is wisdom, but the point pressed at once in v.13 is that with God are wisdom and strength together, and that everything in opposition to him is powerless. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the contrast out in full. It is allowed, he says, that among men there is wisdom and understanding — but it is found only with some few, the ancient and those blessed with length of days, who get it slowly by long experience; and when at last they have the wisdom, they have lost the strength to execute what it designs.

That, for Henry, is exactly the measure of the difference. "With God are both wisdom and strength" — wisdom to design the best and strength to accomplish what is designed; he does not, like aged men, get his counsel by observation, but has it essentially and eternally in himself. "What is the wisdom of ancient men," Henry asks, "compared with the wisdom of the Ancient of days?" So the witnesses agree in reading the verse not as a tribute for its own sake but as a stepping-stone. Job grants the friends, and grants the venerable tradition they lean on, all that can fairly be claimed for grey hairs and long years; and then he lets that best of human wisdom shrink to nothing beside the wisdom that is God's by nature. The aged know much, and Job will not despise it — but their knowledge is borrowed, partial, and outlived, where God's is his own, entire, and everlasting, and it is to that wisdom, not the fathers', that the argument now turns.
13:
"With him is wisdom and strength, he hath counsel and understanding" — and the witnesses read the verse as the crown set upon the foregoing contrast, the moment Job lifts his eyes from the wisest of men to the God who is wisdom itself. The reformed John Gill insists the words belong not to the ancient long-lived man but to God, who made the universe and holds all creatures at his disposal. With him wisdom dwells originally, essentially, and underived, as the very fountain and fulness of it; he is the only and all-wise God, and his wisdom is displayed in framing the world in its beautiful order, in every dispensation of providence which carries a depth of counsel in it, and above all in the work of redemption, wherein he abounded in all wisdom and prudence — so that the Gospel itself is called the wisdom of God. And this wisdom, Gill adds, he has to communicate to his people, to direct them how to carry themselves under every providence.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke states the same truth as the headwater of all our good: "all these things come from God; he is the Fountain of wisdom and the Source of power. He alone can give us unerring counsel, and understanding to comprehend and act profitably by it." The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry knits the four terms into a single perfection. With men, wisdom and strength are commonly parted — the wise are weak and the strong are foolish — but with God are both: wisdom to design the best, and strength to accomplish what is designed. He does not, like us, gather counsel and understanding by observation, but has them essentially and eternally in himself.

Henry lets the doctrine spill over into comfort and warning at once. "It is but little that we know," he says, "and less that we can do; but God can do every thing, and no thought can be withheld from him." Happy, therefore, are those who have this God for their God, for they have infinite wisdom and strength engaged on their side; and foolish and fruitless are all the attempts of men against him. So the witnesses converge without a seam. The wisdom Job magnifies here is not another degree of the wisdom of the aged but a different kind altogether — not learned, not borrowed, not outlived, but the eternal possession of God, joined to a power equal to every purpose it forms. It is a truth that both silences the friends' pretensions and steadies the sufferer's heart, for the same infinite wisdom that no man can outreach is the wisdom that orders his affliction and will one day unfold its reason.
14:
From God's wisdom Job turns to the irresistibleness of his acts, and the witnesses gather round the twofold picture of a ruin none can rebuild and a prison none can open. The reformed John Gill runs through the instances of "he breaketh down, and it cannot be built again": not so much Babel, which its builders left but which stood on, as Sodom, razed to a perpetual desolation, and Thebes and Tyre and the like never rebuilt, and the kingdoms Jeremiah was set to root out, and the four great monarchies broken at last by the kingdom of Christ. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the two clauses as the plainest proof that God is almighty and everything in opposition to him powerless: if he break down any structure whatever it can never be rebuilt, and if he shut a man up — as in a dungeon or a cistern sealed with a stone, like the pit of Lamentations 3:53 — there can be no opening.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke widens the first clause into a meditation on the finality of God's power. He alone can create, and he alone can destroy; nothing can be annihilated but by the same Power that made it, and though man by chemical art may change the form of matter, to reduce the smallest particle to nothing belongs to God alone. In the course of his providence he breaks down so that none can build again — Clarke points to Nineveh, Babylon, Persepolis, and Tyre, cities broken never to rise, and to the Assyrian, Babylonian, Grecian, and Roman empires dismembered past recovery — and "he shutteth up a man" by often frustrating the best-laid purposes, so that they can never be brought to effect.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott states the reach of it in a line: "God has equal power over the moral and physical world." The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley carries the shutting-up to its darkest length: there is no opening without God's permission — "he shutteth up in the grave, and none can break open those sealed doors; he shutteth up in hell, in chains of darkness, and none can pass that great gulf." So the witnesses do not divide; they read the verse as the sober counterweight to the comfort of the last. The same God whose wisdom and strength are the believer's stay is a God whose ruining hand cannot be reversed and whose prison cannot be forced, and there is therefore no contending with his providence, no rebuilding what he has laid in ruins, no releasing whom he has shut up. It is a power that steadies the trusting and terrifies the proud, and Job means his friends to feel both.
15:
For an instance drawn from nature Job names the waters, held back till the land is parched and loosed till it is drowned, and the witnesses hear in the single verse both the making of the world and its unmaking. The reformed John Gill reads "he withholdeth the waters, and they dry up" of God's laying a restraint upon the sea, gathering its waters into their decreed place at the creation and holding them there, or drawing off the flood so the face of the earth was dry, or binding up the rain in the clouds till the brooks fail as the brook Cherith failed. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fixes the two allusions precisely: the withholding points to the third day's work, when God said, Let the waters be gathered into one place, and the dry land appeared in Genesis 1:9; and the sending out points to the flood, when he broke up the fountains of the great deep and the earth was overturned.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads it the same way — the waters reserved in the clouds withheld, and then the springs and brooks and rivers of the earth, or the deluge itself, loosed to overturn the ground, with a manifest allusion to the general flood. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch simply set the verse in its strophe as another proof of the God who disposes the elements as he pleases, bringing upon a land drought or flood according to his will.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the moral the picture carries. God has the command of the waters — he binds them as in a garment, as Proverbs 30:4 asks who has done, and holds them in the hollow of his hand, as Isaiah 40:12 says — and he can punish the children of men by the defect of them or by the excess. Great droughts are sometimes great judgments, when he withholds the waters and the heaven is as brass and the earth as iron; and great floods are sometimes great judgments, when he raises the waters and overturns the earth, its fruits, and its buildings, a sweeping rain that leaves no food. See, Henry says, how many ways God has of contending with a sinful people, and how utterly unable we are to contend with him. So the witnesses converge: the same waters that God gathered to make the dry land habitable he can withhold to starve it or loose to drown it, and in either extreme the lesson is one — that the elements themselves are but instruments in a hand no man can stay.
16:
"With him is strength and wisdom: the deceived and the deceiver are his" — and the witnesses divide most sharply not over the strength but over that closing pair. The reformed John Gill notes only that the first clause repeats v.13 in different words, ascribing to God the greatest might and the most solid and substantial wisdom. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke, however, presses the Hebrew and finds the repetition only apparent: in v.13 the words were intelligence and fortitude, wisdom guiding the exertions of power; here they are strength and sufficiency, power in its very essence and an eternal potentiality — "he borrows nothing, he derives nothing; as he is self-existent, so is he self-sufficient." As for "the deceived and the deceiver are his," Clarke asks whether it does not reach back to the fall itself: Satan the deceiver, and Adam and Eve the deceived, are alike his — for Satan cannot act without permission, and man, whom the seducer thought to make his own for ever, is claimed as God's peculiar property, the seed of the woman appointed to bruise the serpent's head, so that Christ is not ashamed to call his people brethren, as Hebrews 2:11 says.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the phrase of God's rule over every deceit: the deceived and the deceiver are wholly subject to his disposal; he governs the deceiver and sets bounds to how far his deceits shall reach, and overrules all to his own glory and the accomplishment of his righteous designs — trying the good and punishing the wicked by giving them up to believe lies. "Yet God is not the author of any error or sin, but only the wise and holy governor of it."

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gives the maxim its widest reach. Having strength and wisdom, God knows how to make use not only of those who willingly serve him but even of the foolish and the bad who seem fit for no such service: the simplest deceived are not below his notice, and the subtlest deceivers cannot with all their craft escape his eye. The world is full of deceit, one half of mankind cheating the other, and God suffers it and from both will at last bring glory to himself — when Jacob got the blessing by a fraud the design of God's grace was served, and when Ahab was drawn by a false prophecy to his ruin the design of God's justice was served, and in both the deceived and the deceiver were at his disposal, as Ezekiel 14:9 owns. So the witnesses agree that the line proclaims a sovereignty reaching into the very tangle of human falsehood; and they differ only in reach — whether it looks back, with Clarke, to the first deceiver in Eden, or spreads, with Wesley and Henry, over every liar and dupe in the world — but all guard the one truth Wesley states, that God governs the deceit he never authors.
17:
Job now descends to the great ones of the earth, beginning with the wise whom God strips of their wisdom — "he leadeth counsellors away spoiled, and maketh the judges fools." The reformed John Gill takes the counsellors as those of the greatest knowledge in civil things, whose removal is itself a judgment on a people; God can at once spoil them of all their wisdom, confound their schemes, disappoint their devices, and carry their counsel headlong, so that they are stripped both of the fame and of the fruit of their sagacity. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the events of war into it: through God even the counsellors, the great and chief men, are often led into captivity and found among the spoils, while "he maketh the judges fools" by infatuating them.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch attend to the disputed word rendered "spoiled." It does not mean chained, as the Targum would have it, nor taken as booty, as the Septuagint's "captives"; they render rather "he leadeth away counsellors stripped of their robes," the naked figure of men divested of the very insignia of their office. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads it much the same — the wise counsellors and statesmen by whom kings and kingdoms are ordered are led away as captives in triumph, spoiled either of the wisdom they had or seemed to have, or of the power and dignity they enjoyed — and the judges are made fools both by God's discovering their folly and by his turning their own counsels to their ruin.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gives the stroke its theatre and its warning. God leads counsellors away spoiled as trophies of his victory over them, robbed not only of their honour and wealth but of the very wisdom for which they were celebrated, while his own counsel stands and all their devices are brought to nought; and he makes the judges fools, working on their minds to deprive them of judgment and ordering their affairs so that the issue mocks their designs. The counsel of Ahithophel, Henry recalls, became foolishness, and the princes of Zoan were befooled as Isaiah 19:13 records. "Let not the wise man therefore glory in his wisdom," he urges, "nor the ablest counsellors be proud of their station, but humbly depend upon God for the continuance of their abilities." The witnesses do not divide; they leave the first rank of the mighty — the men whose whole strength lay in their heads — stripped, befooled, and led away, a standing proof that the wisdom of the world holds only at the pleasure of the God who gave it.
18:
The stroke rises from counsellors to kings, whom God unbinds and then binds anew — "he looseth the bond of kings, and girdeth their loins with a girdle." The reformed John Gill weighs which bond is meant: not the fetters kings themselves may wear, but rather the yoke of bondage they lay on their subjects, which God loosens by freeing the oppressed from their arbitrary power; or else their own royal waistband, so that to loose it is to ungird and unking them, stripping them of authority — for God sets up kings and removes them at his pleasure. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the whole of dethronement: God takes away their splendid robes and clothes them with sackcloth, dissolves their authority, permits their subjects to rebel and overthrow the state, and binds them as captives, despoiled of power and liberty — proofs of which, he says, crowd the histories of Israel and of the nations.

The two readings of the second clause the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley draws together: God frees the subjects from that whereby kings bind them — their power, authority, and majesty — and then "girdeth their loins with a girdle," reducing the kings themselves to a mean and servile condition, for servants girded up their loose garments to be fit for attendance; God not only deposes them from their thrones but brings them into slavery. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott offers a different construction of the loosing: "he looseth the confederacy of kings, by which they bind themselves together, and girdeth them to fight against each other," though he grants that others take it of the girdle of servitude set against the girdle of state.

Keil and Delitzsch, opening the strophe here, look ahead to the priest-princes of the next verse and fill in the vocabulary Job draws on — the invincible and firmly-rooted, the tested and ready in speech, the men of tact and judgment — all of whom God can strip and confound, and they note that v.21 is repeated word for word in Psalm 107:40. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the lesson: God unbuckles the belts of kings so that the sword drops from their side and the crown soon follows, and girds their loins with the badge of servitude; "kings are not exempt from God's jurisdiction — to us they are gods, but men to him, and subject to more than the common changes of human life." So the witnesses agree that no height of throne is above the reach of the hand that has been breaking counsellors, and divide only over whether the loosed bond is the yoke kings impose, their own royal girdle, or the league by which kings bind themselves together.
19:
The overturning reaches the sacred and the settled — "he leadeth princes away spoiled, and overthroweth the mighty" — and here the witnesses fall into a genuine dispute over a single word. The reformed John Gill allows both readings: the spoiled may be princes stripped of their dominions and glory, or, as the same Hebrew word bears, "priests," for no office however sacred can protect wicked men — the Septuagint reads "he leads the priests captives" — and from such the law itself perishes, they being spoiled of the knowledge that should instruct the people. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke leans decidedly to the priests: how many, he says, have been spoiled of their power and influence, and how many mighty men overthrown; and if the book was written after the captivity, how many priests of Israel and Judah were led away spoiled in those disastrous wars.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott states the question and settles it the other way: the word is used in both senses, but here the parallelism seems to suit princes better. Then he lifts his eyes from the word to the whole movement of the passage, and reads it as Job's deliberate answer to Eliphaz. This latter half of the chapter, he observes, re-echoes the sentiments Eliphaz had uttered in Job 5:11-16, but instead of giving them the optimist's hopeful turn, Job confesses that his own position is rather one of blank despair. Eliphaz was quite sure he possessed the key to the ways of providence; Job ever fears that his ignorance is so profound as to amount almost to hopelessness.

And this, Ellicott insists, is no defect but the truer faith. Job is the type of a man who has felt the hollowness of a traditional orthodoxy and is feeling his way in thick darkness, sustained nevertheless by an unquenchable faith that there is light and that the light will one day dawn — a character, the sequel will make plain, more acceptable to the God of truth than the confident generalizing of Eliphaz. Job's breadth of view, indeed, far exceeds his friend's: where Eliphaz vaguely generalizes, Job declares that not men only but nations are the subjects of God's guiding providence. So the witnesses hold two things at once — a real division over whether God here spoils princes or priests, and a shared sense that Job is not merely repeating the friends' commonplaces about God's power but bending them toward a darker and deeper truth, that the same almighty hand which the friends invoke to comfort is, to a sufferer who cannot read its reasons, a hand of terror as much as of hope.
20:
Next the eloquent are struck dumb and the aged robbed of judgment — "he removeth away the speech of the trusty, and taketh away the understanding of the aged." The reformed John Gill grounds it in God's ownership of the tongue: speech is his gift, the faculty by which men converse and open their minds, and he who gives can take away, as he does at death, when the state of the dead is a state of silence — or in life, striking a man dumb as he did Zechariah, or confounding speech as at Babel, or suffering a man to say only the contrary of what he intends, as Balaam, who would have cursed Israel and could not. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the same two ways, either by taking away or restraining the gift of utterance, or by taking away the understanding that should direct the speech, and fixes the "trusty" as the wise and experienced counsellors whom the greatest princes trusted.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke drives it home with the old proverb of ruin: "the faithful counsellor and the eloquent orator avail nothing — quos Deus vult perdere, prius dementat, God infatuates those whom he is determined to destroy." He points to the threatened stripping of a state's counsellors in Isaiah 3:1, and reads "the understanding of the aged" of the elders, men marked by both seniority and official authority, who can do no more to save a state God means to destroy than a child who can neither reason nor speak.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch carry the strophe on toward the deep things brought to light, while the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gives the two clauses their sharpest point. Those famed for eloquence and trusted with public business are strangely silenced, so that they cannot speak as they intended, but blunder and falter, or speak the very contrary of their purpose — as Balaam blessed those he was called to curse; "let not the orator therefore be proud of his rhetoric." And the aged, who seem to hold their wisdom by prescription, are deprived of it by the infirmities that make them twice children — for there is, as Ecclesiastes 4:13 says, an old and foolish king. So the witnesses converge on a double humbling that reaches the two things men trust most in counsel: the ready tongue that persuades and the long experience that advises. Both are God's loan, and both he can withdraw in a moment, leaving the trusty speechless and the venerable without a thought worth the hearing.
21:
Job turns to the honoured and the strong — "he poureth contempt upon princes, and weakeneth the strength of the mighty" — and the witnesses take the first clause as the debasing of the proud and the second as a knot of Hebrew imagery. The reformed John Gill limits the contempt to bad princes, not the good to whom honour is due, nor the children of God who are princes in a higher sense, but tyrants who oppress their subjects and persecute the godly — a Herod, a Pilate, the persecuting emperors, the antichristian powers — whom God deposes, reduces to a mean and abject state, or cuts off by shameful deaths, as Herod was eaten of worms. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads it more broadly: God pours contempt on princes by leaving them to do mean things or by altering the opinion men have of them, and commonly none are more abject when they are down than those who were haughty and insolent when they were in power, as Psalm 107:40 declares.

The second clause the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke opens with a naturalist's eye. The word for the mighty, he says, means the compact, the well-strung and sinewy, the same term applied to the crocodile's close-knit frame in Job 40:13; and "weakeneth the strength" is more properly, as the margin has it, "looseth the girdle," so that the reference grows sharper still, for the crocodile is banded from shoulder to tail with rows of square scales like parallel girdles. What is human strength against such a creature? "He that made him can make his sword to approach unto him," as the LORD says in Job 40:19; and God alone can loose the girdles of this mighty one.

So the witnesses read one verse in two keys — the moral debasing of proud rulers and the physical loosing of the strongest sinews — and let them answer to each other. The princes who trusted in their eminence are covered with contempt, and the mighty who trusted in their sinewy strength are unbraced, as easily as one loosens a belt; and in both the lesson is the same that has run through the whole roll of the great, that God takes down whatever men lift up. Neither rank nor muscle is any fence against the hand that has been breaking counsellors and unkinging kings; the God who girds and ungirds at will can pour scorn on the proudest throne and loose the girdle of the strongest frame, and no height of dignity or sinew of power stands one moment longer than he pleases to uphold it.
22:
"He discovereth deep things out of darkness, and bringeth out to light the shadow of death" — and the witnesses part over how far into the dark the phrase reaches, whether into the counsels of God or the plots of men. The reformed John Gill lifts it highest, to the deep things of God himself: the thoughts of his heart, very deep as Psalm 92:5 owns; the deep things which the Spirit searches and reveals in 1 Corinthians 2:10; the decrees of election, redemption, and effectual calling, hid in darkness till discovered by their accomplishment; and the love of God, concealed in his breast from everlasting till brought to light in the gift of his Son. What God alone knows he alone can reveal, and does.

The wesleyan-arminian voices bring the beam down to the dark deeds of men. Adam Clarke allows the words may refer either to God's works in the great deep or to the plots and stratagems of wicked men — conspiracies deeply laid and well concealed, about to be produced into act when death, whose shadow had hidden them, is to glut himself with carnage. John Wesley reads it simply of "the most secret counsels of princes, which are contrived and carried on in the dark," dragged out by God into the open day. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fix the sense within the strophe: there is nothing so finely spun that God cannot make it visible; all the secret plans of the wicked, all their hidden sins and veiled deeds, he brings before the tribunal of the world.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the two ranges into one judgment. God discovers deep things out of darkness — plots closely laid are exposed and defeated, wickedness secretly committed and artfully concealed is brought to light and the guilty to their punishment: secret treasons, of which even a bird of the air may carry the voice, as Ecclesiastes 10:20 warns; secret murders and secret whoredoms; for the very cabinet-councils of princes are open before God's eye, as the king of Syria found when Elisha told the words he spoke in his bedchamber in 2 Kings 6:11. So the witnesses do not so much divide as range along a single beam of light: from the unfathomable counsels of God, which he alone can unseal, down to the darkest scheme a wicked heart can bury, nothing lies so deep in shadow that it is hidden from him or safe from his exposure. The God who orders the fall of empires reads also the whispered plot, and the same hand that shapes the great turns of history drags the buried thing into the day.
23:
"He increaseth the nations, and destroyeth them: he enlargeth the nations, and straiteneth them again" — and with this Job lifts his argument from princes to whole peoples, and the witnesses follow him up to the largest scale of providence. The reformed John Gill instances the nations swept away at the flood, and the seven nations of Canaan increased and then destroyed to make room for Israel, and the four great monarchies, and at last the antichristian states yet to fall. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley states the movement plainly: what Job had said of princes he now applies to nations, whom God increases or diminishes as he pleases.

The other wesleyan-arminian witness, Adam Clarke, finds the moral engine of the rise and fall. Following Good, he renders the first clause "he letteth the nations grow licentious," for pride and fullness of bread and wide commerce breed luxury and profligacy; and when the cup of that iniquity is full, God destroys the nation by bringing against it a people less pampered and more inured to toil. He enlarges nations by permitting an accession of territory, and then shuts them up again within their ancient bounds; and though all this seems to fall out by state intrigue and natural cause, divine inspiration pronounces it the work of God's judgment and mercy, "for it is by him that kings reign, and it is he who putteth down one and raiseth up another."

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott hears in the verse a truth apt to be forgotten and yet the key to much of history. Why are the nations marked with such characteristic differences — the Greeks, the Romans, the Jews of old, the French, the English, the Germans of our own day? Why does the counsel of the wisest sometimes fail, as Ahithophel's did, and the bravery of the boldest forsake them? Because there is One working underneath it all for his own ends and glory, as seems him good. Zophar, Ellicott judges, had scarcely risen to this truth; Job holds that there is always a deeper depth, inscrutable, and therefore, from its very darkness, calling for faith. His teaching may seem to savour of fatalism, but only because he handles one side of the problem; had he found occasion, Ellicott adds, he would have stated with equal force the responsibility of man, clay though he be in the potter's hand — for otherwise how should God judge the world? The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry closes the circle: kingdoms have their waxings and wanings, and both are from God, who enlarges their bounds till they make a figure among the nations and then straitens them till the head becomes the tail, as Psalm 107:38 sings. The witnesses do not divide; they widen Job's vision to its horizon, where the same hand that unkings a man and unbraces the mighty is seen swelling and shrinking empires at will, so that the whole march of history is only the outworking of a sovereignty too deep for the friends' shallow reckoning.
24:
Job comes to the leaders of the peoples, whom God empties of heart and sets adrift — "he taketh away the heart of the chief of the people of the earth, and causeth them to wander in a wilderness where there is no way." The reformed John Gill reads the "people of the earth" as the common people and their "chief" or heads as kings, princes, and generals, whose heart is taken away when they are so dispirited as to lose both courage and conduct, having neither the valour nor the skill to defend themselves and their people. He weighs Sephorno's turn, that this was fulfilled in Sihon and Og, whose hearts God hardened to their ruin, but thinks it better applied to the Israelites and their leaders discomfited by the Amalekites soon after they came out of Egypt, about the age in which Job lived.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fastens on the wandering and hears in it a plain allusion to Israel's own history. God suddenly deprives the leaders of courage, so that, panic-struck, they flee when none pursues or are confounded on the eve of great designs; and "he causeth them to wander in a wilderness" recalls the journeyings of Israel in the deserts of Arabia, when their chief, Aaron, had his courage taken from him by the clamours of the people and made them a molten calf, the very defection that cost them near forty years of wandering in a trackless waste. Clarke notes that Houbigant and some others would refer the words rather to the heads of families who led out colonies into distant lands, but he finds the allusion to Israel too apt to be doubted.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets the verse among God's great changes upon the mighty, reading it of those who were bold and courageous and made nothing of dangers, yet are strangely cowed and dispirited when God takes away their heart, so that they become heartless and ready to flee at the shaking of a leaf, as Psalm 66:5 bids us come and see the terrible works of God among the children of men. So the witnesses converge on the strangest of God's strokes upon the great. He has spoiled the counsellor of wisdom, silenced the orator, unkinged the king, and unbraced the mighty; now he reaches into the very courage of the leader, and by simply withdrawing heart leaves the boldest captain a wandering, purposeless man, lost in a pathless waste. Whether the picture points, with Clarke, straight at Aaron and the wilderness years, or spreads over every dispirited chief, the lesson is one: the resolve that armies lean on is itself a gift, and God has only to take away the heart to turn a leader of nations into a lost man groping for a road that is not there.
25:
The chapter ends with the leaders left groping and reeling — "they grope in the dark without light, and he maketh them to stagger like a drunken man" — and the witnesses hear in the close both an echo of Israel's judgments and the summing note of the whole discourse. The reformed John Gill reads them as blind men feeling their way, like the men of Sodom struck blind at Lot's door, or the Egyptians in the gross darkness that might be felt, so that they grope after light and find none. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke traces the very words to Moses, who warned that the LORD would smite a people with madness and blindness, so that they should grope at noonday as the blind gropeth in darkness, in Deuteronomy 28:28; and he finds the staggering borrowed from the sailors of Psalm 107:27, who reel to and fro and stagger like a drunken man.

Clarke closes the chapter with Good's fine reflection on the whole passage, that its imagery is drawn from the machinery of a regular government — its monarchs and princes, its counsellors and judges, its orators and elders, its nobles and its stout peasantry, and even the villains who plot its ruin — and that all of these, with the nations themselves and their heads, are equally in the hands of the Almighty: with him, Good sums it, "human pomp is poverty; human excellence, turpitude; human judgment, error; human wisdom, folly; human dignity, contempt; human strength, weakness." The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley draws the same lesson upward: "thus are the revolutions of kingdoms brought about by an overruling providence; heaven and earth are shaken, but the Lord remaineth a king for ever."

So the witnesses let the chapter end where Job's argument had been driving all along. The greatest of men — the wise, the eloquent, the crowned, the mighty, the leaders of whole peoples — are shown at the last groping and staggering like blind and drunken men, and every prop of human counsel and courage and dignity is seen to hold only while God upholds it. It is a vision that dwarfs the friends' tidy doctrine of desert; for if God so tosses the great ones of the earth, plainly the fortunes of a single sufferer are no simple ledger of his righteousness, but lie hidden, like all these things, in the deep and sovereign wisdom that Job has magnified from first to last. The chapter that opened with the mockery of friends closes with the majesty of God, and leaves the last word not with the confident comforters but with the LORD who reigns for ever over a world too great for them to read.
